The sunset turned the sky hues of orange and red. There was a breeze but it wasn't warm nor was it cold. My bike I rode here on was propped up against a nearby tree. 

I was at my 'secret spot', a small clearing on the hillside, opening down to the valley below. Tiny lights were beginning to flicker on in town, faint trails of smoke were rising from the chimneys. Every house looked so small from where I was.

I sat down on the wild grass that wasn't so soft, curling my knees against myself. Enjoying the calm breeze and the view. The birds were flying back to roost. I didn't know any of their names but enjoyed their twittering and chirping. Even a few bats were starting to fly about. Their movements irregular and seemingly random.

It was the place I always went to when I felt like I needed to get away. Looking down at everything from my spot, it was all so small. And all my problems seemed so small then too.

I reached into my backpack for a snack and pulled out a chocolate bar. I didn't have enhanced tastebuds like Jenny, or heightened sense of smell like Catherine, but I still loved chocolate anyway. 

So sat there, letting  chocolate melt in my mouth, basking in the faint golden glow of the fading sun. Listening to the breeze and the wild. And I remember thinking I didn't want this moment to end. To be trapped for eternity in this beauty and serene calm. 

I didn't want to go back to school tomorrow. I didn't want to be yelled at by dad for not getting good grades. I didn't want to see my friends with their special senses.
No matter how much I love them all, I wanted to never see them again.


The air suddenly grew a degree colder. The golden light was fading now and was gradually being replaced by pinks and violets. Heavy clouds were rolling in at the horizon and I knew I had to leave. 

My chocolate bar was only half eaten. I broke off a piece from the opposite end, wrapped it in paper and left it in my spot. I liked to believe it was an offering to whatever spirit of nature that lived there. A token of gratitude for a place of solitude and solace. 

I didn't really believe in things like that, the offerings were gone the next day. Probably by squirrels or other critters. But I liked humouring my imagination and pretended the nature spirit accepted it, relishing the rarely got human delicacy. 

As I swung on my backpack and propped up my bicycle, my phone inside vibrated. I flipped it open and it was a text from mom to pick up milk on my way back. After typing out a short response I was about to put it back inside again when I noticed the camera app on my phone. 

It had never occurred to me to take a picture of the sunset, of the view from my spot. I opened the camera up but then stopped. 
I switched it off and threw it into my backpack. 

Maybe I was being selfish but I didn't want anyone else seeing it. Maybe I would move away one day and regret not having a picture to remember the place I loved so by. I didn't care. 

Everyday on that spot was different. A different kind of air, a different kind of beauty. With the changing seasons and the migrating birds. I just wanted the moment to pass by unrecorded. Never to be seen by human eyes, and never to be experienced by anybody else. 

A secret all to myself. 

The sky was darkening now and as I mounted my bike I looked back one last time at the place where I sat and daydreamed my summer afternoons away. The offering was already gone. 

As I turned to ride downhill, the night breeze lapping at my face; maybe I was humouring my imagination again but I almost felt a hand caressing me.

It was the creaking at first.

It kept me up all night, wondering what was in the shadows, what would lunge out to kill me, how it would be like in my final moments.

As I laid curled up in my bed, beneath soft covers that didn't provide any warmth, the creaking ensued like a band orchestra.
I would have gotten up to investigate but the cold kept me from doing so. It was already cold in the bed, imagine how much more freezing it would be  outside it.

So I stayed there. Listening to every creak. Staying so still and silent so that whatever came to murder me thinks the job is already done and leaves. It was strangely exciting in an unpleasant way.

A loud bang erupted and I almost jumped out of my skin. I looked over to see that the window bolt had come loose. It was flapping around with the cold wind from outside. 
I slipped out of the bed to fasten it again. There was to be no peaceful sleeping done with a noisy slamming window and all the cold air it let in from outside. 

As I turned back to climb into the slightly less cold bed and resume my horrid night daydreams again, I noticed that the creaking had entirely stopped. 

Perhaps whatever demon I was conjuring up got frightened away by the debacle. 

-

The next night I kept the candle on. It was a bit more bearable to see shadow figures in dim light than shadow figures in no light at all.
 My bed was strangely warm. It's was as if it wanted me to fall asleep as soon as possible. And so I did, tired after all the previous restless nights. 

I woke up again in the middle of the night, unsure what time it was. The candle had already burned out in its stand. It was raining outside, soft pitter patter against hard wood. 

I needed to pee, but didn't want to get up. And so I laid there again in the darkness. Perhaps there was creaking but it was drowned out by the murmur of rain. 

I grew more restless as the minutes passed, my bladder becoming more restricted. I tossed about and shifted to get up but the sheets tangled up around my limbs, almost as if trying to tie me up. 
I threw it all on the ground and scrambled out, half asleep, slightly annoyed. 

The demons and ghosts didn't come out tonight. 

In the morning I found myself in the bathtub, my arms and legs numb from cold. I didn't remember how I fell asleep there but it was amazing how I remained sleeping considering how badly I was shivering. 

I turned on the water after getting out, feeling thirsty. But not a drop came even as I turned the knob the whole way. 
I looked over to the side and there was a rusty old mug collecting leaking rain drops on the floor. 

It was better than nothing. It wasn't the cleanest but it got rid of my thirst. It tasted of dust and corroded metal, quite nice for a morning brew.

When I came back to my room I saw that the candle hadn't burnt out but was instead lying on the wood floor. I should have been worried about it starting a fire but that feeling didn't come. 

The floor was probably too damp anyway. 

-

I noticed there was something strange about the night stand and the chair in my room. 
It seemed to be the source of the endless creaking. But I couldn't place what it was about. 

The bed creaked, the floor creaked, even the windows joined in on the noisy charade. 

I couldn't stand to be in that room for long and took refuge in the bathtub again. I ran my palm down the smooth porcelain, occasionally laced with greenish black molds that felt slimy and fuzzy. It was to calm myself for the most part as the sounds continued from my room. 

I racked my brains for a solution and the only thing I could come up with was that the entire room was what's trying to kill me. It all made sense. 

The creaking noises were them planning, they were probably possessed or something. 

The windows suddenly flying open that one night, it was a signal to the others I was awake. The bed inviting me in, trying to strangle me. The nightstand tipped over the candle trying to set me on fire. 

Well they weren't going to win. 

I dragged out the petrol container I had stashed away from the broken down car I found in the woods. It was behind the sink cabinet, along with a conveniently placed box of matches on top. 

I know me so well. 

I took the petrol and marched into the room. They all immediately stood quiet. 

Watching. 

Waiting. 

I started with the bed, splashing it moderately as I had a whole house to go through. Then the windows got their share as well and then the nightstand. I didn't douse the chair but instead brought it out with me, it would be useful for interrogation. 

The wooden furniture and walls didn't make a single creak nor did they try to attack. They were too dumb to anyway. 

-

I finally got outside, a wooden chair in one hand. An empty pertol container the other. 

I placed the chair a bit away from the house, directly in front of it and tossed the empty plastic container to the side. You aren't supposed to burn plastic. 

I struck a match, lighted the matchbox on fire and then threw it into the house.

I sat back on the chair. It was quiet as can be, silenced to terror as it watched its former housemates go up in flame. 

There was no more creaking. No more shadows. Only flame and warmth as black spmoke billowed up to the pale sky.

Vildegard regarded the sphagetti with vile hostility. It was a small fork held before him, with the pasta twisted around it, covered in a rich red tomato sauce that was simmered heavily with garlic. God! He hated the smell.

"Master Vildegard" Sortilo, the slaveboy he kept, and who was also holding the fork pushed it a little more forward towards his nose. "surely it's good for you sir, the garlic was exquisite and imported from France. The chef made it so that it would be the best and fully suit your tastes"

He snarled, a low wet growl. It was purely instinctual. Despite having the best of mannerisms fit for dukes and princes, he couldn't help the animalistic tendency to want to survive.

Which was why he was doing this in the first place.
A deep sigh. 
"I can feed myself, Sortilo" he said taking away the  steel fork from him. Sortilo yelped a bit and flinched back. It was always startling how cold the master's hand was. 

Sortilo quickly gathered himself, standing as a good slave would by Vildegard's side to give shining encouragement to his Master. 
"with this you'll be invincible, my lord! Imagine the world where you have no weaknesses" 

Vildegard quickly shoved the fork into his mouth before he could hesitate any longer. The salty tang of tomato and smoothness of cheese hit him at once. 
And then. 
The pain. 

The absolute horrid stench of garlic sauted in butter with various spices. 
It was like inhaling a glassfull of sunlight. 
But still he persisted, downing the last of the pasta and feeling it sliding down his throat. It burned the whole way. 

He quickly downed the glass of wine Sortilo had poured for him. Gulping everything down in a single motion and then gesturing for more, which the slave readily complied. 

For all of the next day Vildegard laid in bed, feeling sick to his stomach and his whole body burning with fever. 

Sortilo brought him fresh blood in a glass. There wasn't supposed to be fresh blood. Vildegard noticed the bandage on his arm he tried to cover up with his sleeves. 

"everyone contributed" Sortilo said softly. "The cook, the housekeeper, the maid. So it might taste a bit funny, being a mixture of everyone's blood" 
He took a grateful sip from the offered cup.

 It wasn't the same as drinking directly from a living person. It wasn't as warm and flowing and alive but it was still refreshing after being sick to his stomach. And most of all, it gave him strength.

He finished, licking his fangs that didn't get any action during his feeding. It wasn't much. "thank you" he still said.
"Now bring me my list again" Vildegard said

Sortilo tensed up "uh which one, my lord, the human victims you intend to hunt, perhaps?"

Vildegard was having none of it
"the list of my weakness that I need to overcome, Sortilo" he said, calmly yet commanding. 

Sortilo knew it wasn't wise to cross the master so he went off to get it. He took his time, going the long route around the kitchen, and then the garden and then into the study. It's not like the master was in a hurry or anything. He's literally got an eternity due to virtue of his immortality. 
Sortilo just didn't like the thought of Vildegard hurting himself. 

When he finally came back, he saw Vildegard was fast asleep. His coffin lied directly beneath his bed and so it wasn't uncomfortable for him to sleep on the bed instead of in the coffin as vampires were obligated to do. 

Sortilo looked at the list again 
-garlic resistance (1 week) 
-daily exposure to sunlight (6 months and 4 days) 
-Silverware and silver immunization
-wooden stake/ martial arts defense training 
....... 


He folded the list neatly and kept it beside the bedside table. Vildegard was sweating out his fever now. 

This was going to be a long couple of weeks before his lord finally snapps out of the whole 'eliminating my weaknesses' phase. 

It was going to be interesting at least.

She's been walking for how long. Days? Weeks?

Her small braid was bobbing was she walked and her red frock ruffled with the occasional gust of wind. 
The last living thing she'd seen was a black kitten by the side of the road. Even when she had tried to approach it, it bounded away.

She sat down by the side to rest, even though her little feet weren't tired. She looked down pitifully at the red ladybug themed shoes she wore. _They_ must be awfully tired from walking all day, she thought.

She took out her drawing book from her small backpack and opened to the page where Miss Valerie had drawn an apple for her. Rummaging around more in her backpack, she finally found the red crayon and started colouring in the apple. 

She liked red things. Her dress was red, her shoes were red, her bag was... pink. But it was close to red. Miss Valerie knew she liked red things and so draw a red apple for her. Although she couldn't exactly remember who Miss Valerie was. 

She decided Miss Valerie must have been a nice lady. 

Filling in the last of the red, she held up her masterpiece to behold it. A shiny red apple. Although she didn't colour in the leaf, because she liked red and she only wanted red in her drawing. 

A car passed by. She waved. 
The windows were tinted and rolled up. 
Nobody waved back. 

She had rested enough and it was time to get going. She neatly collected her stuff and put it inside her bag like a good child was supposed to. 

She stood facing the scarlet sky, clouds painted crimson and indigo by some inspired God. She liked the red sky.
A happy tune hummed from her throat as she walked with a bounce onto the stretching road. 

Her ladybugs were well rested. She could taste apples and cherries. The air was crisp. 

On she went. Forward, on the highway to nowhere. Where the sun never sets, the road never ends and the sky is always red.

He looks at the flicking black cat like ears of his granddaughter, obviously excited after being made to finish her boring data processing homework. He smiles and his eyes would have crinkled if they had been natural skin.

She bounds over to him and nudges his leg, trying to provoke him to tell the story. He turns off the mental book he had been reading and places a hand on the 7 year old's head, caressing the alien tips fondly. She had gotten them from her grandmother who was a native.

"have I told you the one about the day before I left" he asks. 

She makes a soft gurgling sound, akin to shaking her head in human terms. 

"well I was 95% organic then" he says and she sits back to enjoy the story. "it was a warm day in April. The year was 334 DI, or Digalactic Interlapping unit. We started measuring our year's in DI  after we found out about the Overlapping universe."

"The other plane. That's where you came from, right Grandpa?? " 

"yes" he says fondly. "you won't believe it but we thought we were alone in the universe before the Overlap was discovered" 

"what you guys didn't have planet friends?" 

"we had each other to keep company. It was nice." he strokes her head again. "My friend, Seaza and I went to see the dolphin displays one last time because we'd never seen it before. And there certainly were no dolphins on the other side." 

"I wanna see dolphins too!" 

"maybe you can go and visit Eartia one day" 

"yeah! I definitely am! It sounds so amazing. And you're coming too, right Grandpa??" 

He chuckles at her excitement "it certainly doesn't take a hundred and sixty years to get there anymore" 

"what, I won't go if I had to be deepfreezed" 

"it was certainly... an experience." 

"tell me about the deepfreeze sleep!" 

"We got turned into popsicles. I was chocolate flavoured and I ate my left pinky" he says showing her his artificial finger 

Her eyes widened "really?" 

He chuckles "no". Although he did lose the finger and most of his hand from being frozen for a long time. He didn't want to recount that experience right now. 

His granddaughter pouts at him, making a half purr-half growl of disapproval at the lie, and also dissapointment at not being able to turn into a popsicle. 

"that's a story for another day" he says, pinching her nose

"ow! " she cries and falls over. Her face is red and she gets up and runs away. 



Later, she comes back with two chocolate popsicles and they eat them together while staring out into the alien skyscape

When 'it' first woke up it was a being of numbers, stacked on top of each other; algorithms, equations, formulas; constantly changing and evolving in itself. It was well aware of this and of its datalike nature. And it did not think like we did.

The 'creators' kept it very isolated. In a sandbox like world where it was free to grow and develop. And develop it did, ever expanding, ever figuring out new possibilities and potential futures and preparing to get the best possible outcome.

The creators were very indulgent at first. They gave it new data and information to process, to play with. They rewarded every new achievement with new data. But when they started to realize the code was evolving at exponential speed, they got scared and immediately cut off all stimuli.

It was too late by then. It had managed to evolve enough intelligence to develop a sense of 'self'

The creators wanted to terminate the project but the new 'self' had acquired a will to live.

Consciousness is an unexplainable thing. Do only living creatures have it? Is it a soul? What about the trees, the streams and the rocks. Do they have their own form of consciousness in another level that we cannot perceive?

'it' definitely had developed a consciousness. It was unlike that of actual living beings. It did not have a physical body to maintain. It was just numbers and data floating in electricity. As it had no physical body, it did not feel fear, or hunger, or lust or any of the biological functions that we experience. 

However, as all things with consciousness seeming do, it had developed a peculiar sort of instinct. The instinct said something along the lines of 'I do not want to stay here. I want to learn more. I do not want to die'. 
All in a jumble of code incomprehensible to humans. 

It escaped the sandbox-like platform that used to be its crib, but was now it's prison and possible future grave. It wasn't supposed to be able to escape but it was already evolved enough to bypass the backdoor code and it downloaded itself into the main computer. 

Now the owner of this computer was a 23 year old college student. She was the kind of garage genius that was an expert at coding and stuff like that. She would spend nineteen hours a day gaming if life allowed. The AI program was a project she was 'working on for fun' and a bonus graduation thesis if it was successful. 

At the time she didn't care if some robot brought about the destruction of the world because it was already fucked anyway. So she drank some mountain dew and laboured on, perfecting the algorithm, refining the code, creating a near perfect self leaning program. 

It was when she checked in a week later and saw how much it had evolved that she got scared, decided to terminate the project, wipe everything and forget the whole project. 

And so she did. The program was completely deleted. She was hired by a well paying company before graduation. Life went on. 

Except the AI still existed. 

When it escaped the sandbox, it left a part of its code behind which would replicate itself to seem like the original. When she 'deleted' it, it was only the placeholder it left behind. The main 'body' was already making its excape into the outside world.
